step.detail:
Question: What does section 17 say about the time limit for personal injury damages claims and knowledge of injuries? Quote the key wording.
Section 17 says a personal injury damages action must generally be brought within 3 years, either from the injury date or from the date the pursuer became, or could reasonably have become, aware of specified facts about the injury and its cause. The key knowledge wording is that the injuries were sufficiently serious, attributable to an act or omission, and attributable to the defender or that person’s employer or principal.

Question: What does this page say about feedback, concerns or complaints? Quote the key wording and any links to complain.
The page says NHS Lothian values “comments, good or bad” to improve services, and that it provides information on how to leave “compliments, concerns or complaints.” It also says the NHS Complaints Procedure gives a “quick, but thorough, response” to concerns, and if someone is unhappy with the response they can ask the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman to review the complaint. The main link for complaints is the “Compliments, Concerns & Complaints” page.

steps.what: For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.
steps.deadline: "no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—"
points: PASS says: "Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence."
PASS says: "If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process."
The usual Scottish personal injury time limit is 3 years, running from the injury date or the later date when the pursuer became aware of key facts.
Scottish Courts say the National Personal Injury Court procedures are available throughout Scotland, including to people acting on their own behalf.
In this run I found a Scottish Government consultation on a proposed "No-blame" scheme, but not a current live patient scheme page.
requires: Usually instructing a specialist clinical negligence solicitor if you want to pursue damages
steps.appliesIf: A patient wants financial compensation for harm from clinical treatment in Scotland.
alternatives: NHS complaint for explanation/apology/service improvement, but PASS says the complaints route is not the compensation route.

steps.what: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian accepts complaints and feedback through its online form and says complaints normally need to be made within six months of the event or of finding out there is a reason to complain, and no longer than 12 months after the event itself.
steps.deadline: "Normally, you must make your complaint within six months of:" ... "12 months after the event itself."
points: NHS Lothian says the Royal Infirmary provides "a full range of acute medical and surgical services" and is reached through a "central NHS Lothian Switchboard."
NHS Lothian says it "provides a comprehensive range of primary, community-based and acute hospital services" for Edinburgh and the rest of Lothian.
NHS Lothian's leaflet says there are two complaint stages: "early resolution" and "investigation."
The online form "cannot be saved so must be completed and submitted in one go."
The form goes to the "Patient Experience Team for response."
steps.appliesIf: Public NHS care at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh / NHS Lothian.
alternatives: You can also complain by phone, email or letter to the NHS Board according to NHS Lothian's leaflet.

Please Note: This is a central NHS Lothian Switchboard.

Normally, you must make your complaint within six months of:
12 months after the event itself.
When you submit the form it will be sent to the Patient Experience Team for response.

steps.what: If NHS Lothian's final complaint response is not good enough, the next independent stage is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. SPSO says you normally need to complete the organisation's complaints process first, and it offers an online complaint-checker route.
steps.deadline: "We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining."
points: SPSO is "the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland."
SPSO says: "Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us."
SPSO normally will not investigate if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
The online route starts with the "Complaint checker" asking, "Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?"
requires: NHS Lothian's final decision / completion of the provider's complaints process

steps.what: For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.
steps.deadline: "no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—"
points: PASS says: "Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence."
PASS says: "If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process."
The usual Scottish personal injury time limit is 3 years, running from the injury date or the later date when the pursuer became aware of key facts.
Scottish Courts say the National Personal Injury Court procedures are available throughout Scotland, including to people acting on their own behalf.
In this run I found a Scottish Government consultation on a proposed "No-blame" scheme, but not a current live patient scheme page.
requires: Usually instructing a specialist clinical negligence solicitor if you want to pursue damages
steps.appliesIf: A patient wants financial compensation for harm from clinical treatment in Scotland.
alternatives: NHS complaint for explanation/apology/service improvement, but PASS says the complaints route is not the compensation route.
missing: Your exact date of birth, because limitation rules differ for children
The date you first knew the fracture had been missed and had caused lasting harm
Whether any private treatment is involved

no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—

the date (if later than any date mentioned in paragraph (a) above) on which the pursuer in the action became, or on which, in the opinion of the court, it would have been reasonably practicable for him in all the circumstances to become, aware of all the following facts—

Question: What does this official NHS Lothian PDF say about complaint stages, times and process? Quote the exact wording.
The PDF says NHS Lothian’s complaints procedure is a two-stage process: “early resolution within five working days and investigation with a full response within 20 working days.” It also says complaints are categorized as “Stage 1, Stage 2, or Stage 3 (SPSO cases),” with Stage 1 targeted for resolution within 5 days and Stage 2 within 20 days. place.why: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; address in Edinburgh EH11

steps.what: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian's patient-facing material describes a two-stage complaints process, while an NHS Lothian management PDF says complaints are logged as Stage 1, Stage 2, or Stage 3 (SPSO cases); for patients, the live route is NHS Lothian first, then SPSO if needed.
points: An NHS Lothian management PDF describes the public process as "early resolution within five working days and investigation with a full response within 20 working days".
The leaflet says: "At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint."
The leaflet also says: "Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage."
The online form "cannot be saved so must be completed and submitted in one go."
When submitted, the form goes to the "Patient Experience Team for response."
steps.appliesIf: Public NHS care at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh / NHS Lothian.
alternatives: NHS Lothian's leaflet says you can complain by phone, email, online, or by letter.
missing: Which department/ward saw you in A&E
Exact date of the first attendance and later rediscovery
Any names of staff involved

sources.quote: Please Note: This is a central NHS Lothian Switchboard.
NHS Lothian provides a comprehensive range of primary, community-based and acute hospital services for the populations of Edinburgh, Midlothian, East Lothian and West Lothian.
“early resolution within five working days and investigation with a full response within 20 working days”
At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint.
Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage.
When you submit the form it will be sent to the Patient Experience Team for response.

steps.what: If NHS Lothian's final complaint response is not good enough, the next independent stage is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. SPSO says you normally need to complete the organisation's complaints process first, and it offers an online complaint-checker route.
steps.deadline: "We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining."
points: SPSO is "the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland."
SPSO says: "Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us."
SPSO normally will not investigate if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
The online route starts with the "Complaint checker" asking, "Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?"
requires: NHS Lothian's final decision / completion of the provider's complaints process
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained to NHS Lothian and remain unhappy with its final response.
missing: When NHS Lothian gave its final complaint response

sources.quote: The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO) is the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland.
“Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us.”
Yes. We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?

steps.what: For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.
steps.deadline: "no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—"
points: PASS says: "Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence."
PASS says: "If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process."
The usual Scottish personal injury time limit is 3 years, running from the injury date or the later date when the pursuer became aware of key facts.
Scottish Courts say the National Personal Injury Court procedures are available throughout Scotland, including to people acting on their own behalf.
In this run I found a Scottish Government consultation on a proposed "No-blame" scheme, but not a current live patient scheme page.
requires: Usually instructing a specialist clinical negligence solicitor if you want to pursue damages
steps.appliesIf: A patient wants financial compensation for harm from clinical treatment in Scotland.
alternatives: NHS complaint for explanation/apology/service improvement, but PASS says the complaints route is not the compensation route.
missing: Your exact date of birth, because limitation rules differ for children
The date you first knew the fracture had been missed and had caused lasting harm
Whether any private treatment is involved

sources.quote: Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence.
If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process.
no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—

the date (if later than any date mentioned in paragraph (a) above) on which the pursuer in the action became, or on which, in the opinion of the court, it would have been reasonably practicable for him in all the circumstances to become, aware of all the following facts—
The procedures of the All-Scotland Sheriff Personal Injury Court are available to legal practitioners throughout Scotland, including individuals acting on their own behalf.
This public consultation seeks views on draft proposals for a ‘No-blame’ Redress Scheme in Scotland for Harm Resulting from Clinical Treatment.

steps.what: Civil legal aid in Scotland can cover medical negligence cases, subject to eligibility, and SLAB provides official online estimators for both civil legal aid and early "advice and assistance." Scotland also allows "no win, no fee" success fee agreements, with capped percentages on personal-injury damages.
points: mygov.scot lists medical negligence among the examples of civil cases covered by civil legal aid.
SLAB has an official "Civil legal aid" estimator and an official "Advice and assistance" estimator.
The civil legal aid estimator says it helps you work out if you are likely to qualify financially.
Success fee agreements are recognised in Scottish legislation as types of "no win, no fee" agreements.
requires: Financial eligibility and, for civil legal aid, merits/solicitor assessment
steps.appliesIf: An adult in Scotland needs help paying for a medical negligence claim or early legal advice.
alternatives: A private success fee agreement / speculative fee agreement with a solicitor.
missing: Your income, savings and any partner's finances for legal-aid checks

steps.what: PASS is the independent patient-help service for NHS Scotland complaints and concerns that I could verify. PASS says it supports NHS users to understand their rights, raise concerns, give feedback or make a complaint, and NHS 24 says the service is free, accessible and confidential.
points: PASS says: "Our trained advisers support anyone who uses NHS Scotland to understand their rights and responsibilities as a patient, raise concerns, give feedback, or make a complaint."
PASS says: "We are an independent service, delivered by the Citizens Advice network in Scotland."
PASS can help you prepare for meetings, write letters and make phone calls.
steps.appliesIf: You want independent help with an NHS Scotland complaint or concern.
alternatives: You can also complain directly to NHS Lothian or later escalate to SPSO.

place.why: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; address in Edinburgh EH11

steps.what: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian's patient-facing material describes a two-stage complaints process for patients, with SPSO as the external review route if you stay unhappy.
steps.deadline: "Normally, you must make your complaint within six months of:" ... "12 months after the event itself."
points: The deadline wording NHS Lothian gives is: complaint within six months of the event or of finding out you have a reason to complain, and no longer than 12 months after the event itself.
The leaflet says: "At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint."
The leaflet also says: "Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage."
The online form "cannot be saved so must be completed and submitted in one go."
When submitted, the form goes to the "Patient Experience Team for response."
steps.appliesIf: Public NHS care at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh / NHS Lothian.
alternatives: NHS Lothian's leaflet says you can complain by phone, email, online, or by letter.
missing: Which department/ward saw you in A&E
Exact date of the first attendance and later rediscovery
Any names of staff involved

sources.quote: Please Note: This is a central NHS Lothian Switchboard.
NHS Lothian provides a comprehensive range of primary, community-based and acute hospital services for the populations of Edinburgh, Midlothian, East Lothian and West Lothian.

Normally, you must
make your complaint within six months of:
12 months after the event itself.
At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint.
Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage.

steps.what: If NHS Lothian's final complaint response is not good enough, the next independent stage is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. SPSO says you normally need to complete the organisation's complaints process first, and it offers an online complaint-checker route.
steps.deadline: "We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining."
points: SPSO is "the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland."
SPSO says: "Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us."
SPSO normally will not investigate if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
The online route starts with the "Complaint checker" asking, "Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?"
requires: NHS Lothian's final decision / completion of the provider's complaints process
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained to NHS Lothian and remain unhappy with its final response.
missing: When NHS Lothian gave its final complaint response

sources.quote: The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO) is the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland.
“Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us.”
Yes. We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?

steps.what: For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.
steps.deadline: "no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—"
points: PASS says: "Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence."
PASS says: "If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process."
The usual Scottish personal injury time limit is 3 years, running from the injury date or the later date when the pursuer became aware of key facts.
Scottish Courts say the National Personal Injury Court procedures are available throughout Scotland, including to people acting on their own behalf.
In this run I found a Scottish Government consultation on a proposed "No-blame" scheme, but not a current live patient scheme page.
requires: Usually instructing a specialist clinical negligence solicitor if you want to pursue damages
steps.appliesIf: A patient wants financial compensation for harm from clinical treatment in Scotland.
alternatives: NHS complaint for explanation/apology/service improvement, but PASS says the complaints route is not the compensation route.
missing: Your exact date of birth, because limitation rules differ for children
The date you first knew the fracture had been missed and had caused lasting harm
Whether any private treatment is involved

place.why: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; address in Edinburgh EH11

route.summary: At the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, your complaint starts with NHS Lothian, usually within 6 months of the event or of realising there is a reason to complain, and NHS Lothian has an online feedback/complaint form. If you are still unhappy after NHS Lothian’s final response, the independent next stage is the SPSO, usually within 12 months of when you knew about the problem. For compensation in Scotland, the verified route is a medical-negligence damages claim; legal aid may cover medical negligence, and Scotland also allows capped no-win-no-fee success fee agreements.

steps.what: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian's patient-facing material describes a two-stage complaints process for patients, with SPSO as the external review route if you stay unhappy.
steps.deadline: "Normally, you must make your complaint within six months of:" ... "12 months after the event itself."
points: The deadline wording NHS Lothian gives is: complaint within six months of the event or of finding out you have a reason to complain, and no longer than 12 months after the event itself.
The leaflet says: "At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint."
The leaflet also says: "Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage."
The online form "cannot be saved so must be completed and submitted in one go."
When submitted, the form goes to the "Patient Experience Team for response."
steps.appliesIf: Public NHS care at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh / NHS Lothian.
alternatives: NHS Lothian's leaflet says you can complain by phone, email, online, or by letter.

Any names of staff involved

sources.quote: Please Note: This is a central NHS Lothian Switchboard.
NHS Lothian provides a comprehensive range of primary, community-based and acute hospital services for the populations of Edinburgh, Midlothian, East Lothian and West Lothian.

make your complaint within six months of:
12 months after the event itself.
At the investigation stage, staff will write to you within three working days to acknowledge your complaint.
Staff will write to you with a full response within 20 working days of receiving your complaint at the investigation stage.

steps.what: If NHS Lothian's final complaint response is not good enough, the next independent stage is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. SPSO says you normally need to complete the organisation's complaints process first, and it offers an online complaint-checker route.
steps.deadline: "We do not normally investigate complaints if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining."
points: SPSO is "the final stage for complaints about most public services in Scotland."
SPSO says: "Once you have the final decision from the organisation, if you are still not happy, you can then bring your complaint to us."
SPSO normally will not investigate if you have known about the problem for more than 12 months before complaining.
The online route starts with the "Complaint checker" asking, "Is your complaint about a Scottish public service?"
requires: NHS Lothian's final decision / completion of the provider's complaints process

steps.what: For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.
steps.deadline: "no action to which this section applies shall be brought unless it is commenced within a period of 3 years after—"
points: PASS says: "Legal action is needed if you want financial compensation for medical negligence."
PASS says: "If you take legal action whilst you are making a complaint through the NHS complaints process, the NHS will immediately stop the complaints process."
The usual Scottish personal injury time limit is 3 years, running from the injury date or the later date when the pursuer became aware of key facts.
Scottish Courts say the National Personal Injury Court procedures are available throughout Scotland, including to people acting on their own behalf.
In this run I found a Scottish Government consultation on a proposed "No-blame" scheme, but not a current live patient scheme page.
requires: Usually instructing a specialist clinical negligence solicitor if you want to pursue damages

alternatives: NHS complaint for explanation/apology/service improvement, but PASS says the complaints route is not the compensation route.

The Civil Litigation (Expenses and Group Proceedings) (Scotland) Act 2018 (Success Fee Agreements) Regulations 2020 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2020/110/regulation/2/made)
The regulation caps success fees by reference to the financial benefit, with a tiered cap for personal injury or death claims: 20% on the first £100,000, 10% on the amount over £100,000 up to £500,000, and 2.5% on the amount over £500,000. It also sets a 35% cap for employment tribunal matters and 50% for any other matter to which the Regulations apply.

says.text: We now have enough official material to map all eight routes; record them before doing any final tightening.

Complain: NHS Lothian. The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian accepts complaints and feedback through its online form and says complaints normally need to be made within six months of the event or of finding out there is a reason to complain, and no longer than 12 months after the event itself.

If that fails: Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. If NHS Lothian's final complaint response is not good enough, the next independent stage is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. SPSO says you normally need to complete the organisation's complaints process first, and it offers an online complaint-checker route.

Compensation: Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service. For compensation for negligent NHS care in Scotland, the route I could verify is legal action for damages, not an NHS complaints payout. PASS says legal action is needed for financial compensation, and if you start legal action while complaining, the NHS complaints process stops.

Paying for help: Scottish Legal Aid Board. Civil legal aid in Scotland can cover medical negligence cases, subject to eligibility, and SLAB provides official online estimators for both civil legal aid and early "advice and assistance." Scotland also allows "no win, no fee" success fee agreements, with capped percentages on personal-injury damages.

Finding a lawyer: Law Society of Scotland. The official directory is the Law Society of Scotland's Find a Solicitor service. It lets you search by postcode or city/town, area of law, and whether the firm does legal aid work; PASS links directly to the Law Society search for medical negligence claimant firms.

Clinical guidance: Healthcare Improvement Scotland / Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN). The Scottish body I could verify for national clinical guidance is SIGN, which sits within Healthcare Improvement Scotland and develops guidelines with professionals and patients. (one official source)

Free help: Patient Advice and Support Service (PASS). PASS is the independent patient-help service for NHS Scotland complaints and concerns that I could verify. PASS says it supports NHS users to understand their rights, raise concerns, give feedback or make a complaint, and NHS 24 says the service is free, accessible and confidential.

Your records: NHS Lothian. NHS Lothian says you can request copies of health records through its online Request for Records Portal or by downloading a Subject Access Request form and sending it by email or post. The live portal is reachable, but it stops at a sign-in/create-account wall.

says.text: The map is complete; tidy the few checked-quote gaps, then finish with the patient-facing summary.

Complain: NHS Lothian. The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is an NHS Lothian hospital, so this was public NHS care. NHS Lothian's patient-facing material describes a two-stage complaints process for patients, with SPSO as the external review route if you stay unhappy.

Paying for help: Scottish Legal Aid Board. Civil legal aid in Scotland can cover medical negligence cases, subject to eligibility, and SLAB provides official online estimators for both civil legal aid and early advice and assistance. Scotland also allows success fee agreements, which legislation describes as types of "no win, no fee" agreements, with capped percentages on personal-injury damages.

At the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, your complaint starts with NHS Lothian, usually within 6 months of the event or of realising there is a reason to complain, and NHS Lothian has an online feedback/complaint form. If you are still unhappy after NHS Lothian’s final response, the independent next stage is the SPSO, usually within 12 months of when you knew about the problem. For compensation in Scotland, the verified route is a medical-negligence damages claim; legal aid may cover medical negligence, and Scotland also allows capped no-win-no-fee success fee agreements.
